rows.value: Indian passport holders need a B-2 visitor visa for medical treatment, applied for at a US Consulate with a treating-physician letter and proof of funds; interview wait times at Indian consulates have run very long (reported into the hundreds of days for B-2), so plan well ahead. Verify current requirements at travel.state.gov / the US Consulate.

rows.label: From India
rows.value: Roughly 15-17h+ to the US East Coast from DEL/BOM, usually with one stop.

rows.label: Language
rows.value: English throughout; interpreters arranged by hospital international offices on request.

rows.label: Cost context
rows.value: Generally the most expensive destination — often several times Indian prices for equivalent care; chosen for expertise on the hardest cases rather than value.

rows.label: Companion visa
rows.value: Accompanying family or caregivers also travel on their own B-2 visas.

onGround.label: On the ground
onGround.value: Plan around long-haul routing and consulate wait times both. From arrival, hospital international offices help with airport transfers, medically-appropriate hotels or serviced apartments near campus, and interpreters where a language other than English is preferred. Extended-stay residences and hospital-adjacent hotels are the norm for families settling in for weeks. Vegetarian and Jain diets are understood in major cities; a nearby Indian community and restaurants make longer stays easier. Connectivity is excellent throughout.

recovery.label: Recovery & convalescence
recovery.value: Convalescence is typically in a hospital-adjacent hotel or serviced apartment, with outpatient follow-up until you are cleared to fly. For rehabilitation-heavy recovery, dedicated inpatient rehab facilities are attached to or affiliated with the major centres. Many teams now offer virtual follow-up once you return to India.

aroundTreatment.heading: The place, not just the clinic.
aroundTreatment.text: Where families stay, eat and rest while a member is cared for — our city guides for the same destination.

rows.label: JCI accreditation
rows.value: Joint Commission International is the recognised global standard for hospital quality and safety. Accredited organisations are re-evaluated every three years, and more than 1,000 across 70-plus countries hold it. It is a strong baseline signal, though it speaks to process and safety rather than to any single surgeon or outcome.

rows.label: Magnet recognition
rows.value: The ANCC Magnet designation, common in top US hospitals, recognises nursing excellence. It is selective, held by around a tenth of US hospitals, and is linked to better patient outcomes and stable, engaged staff. Nursing quality shapes recovery as much as the surgery itself.

rows.label: The rankings, in context
rows.value: Newsweek's World's Best Hospitals and US News rankings weigh peer reputation, quality measures, patient experience and credentials like JCI and Magnet. They are a useful shortlist, not a verdict on your specific condition. For that, look to a centre's depth in your exact procedure.

rows.label: How to judge for you
rows.value: Beyond the badges, ask about volume in your specific procedure, the named team who would treat you, and their approach to your case. Confirm international-patient services: interpreters, coordination, and dietary needs including vegetarian and Jain. A great hospital for one condition is not automatically great for another.

items: Leave with a complete record: discharge summary, operative notes, medications, pathology, imaging and follow-up plan.
Ask for actual scan files (DICOM), not just the printed report.
Book and brief your Indian specialist before you fly home.
We move records between your teams on your instruction; we never interpret them.

rows.label: The handover is the whole point
rows.value: The best overseas care can unravel on the flight home if nobody in India has the full picture. Before you leave the hospital abroad, the aim is simple: a complete, portable record that your doctor here can read, act on, and continue — medications, follow-up schedule, warning signs and the surgeon's own notes included.

rows.label: What to collect before you leave
rows.value: Discharge summary and operative notes. A clear medication list with doses and durations. Pathology and lab reports. Imaging — ideally the actual scan files (DICOM) on a drive or via a secure link, not only the printed report. The recommended follow-up plan with dates. And direct contact details for the treating team, in case your Indian doctor wants to speak with them.

rows.label: Imaging, done right
rows.value: A printed radiology report is a summary; the images themselves are the evidence. Ask for the raw DICOM files so your doctor in India can review the scans directly and compare them against future ones. Keep a backup copy. Where the hospital offers a secure patient portal or transfer link, use it rather than email.

rows.label: Setting up follow-up at home
rows.value: Line up your Indian specialist before you fly back, and share the records ahead of the first appointment so nothing is read cold. rows.label: Why the stay matters
rows.value: After a major procedure, most patients are discharged from the ward long before they are ready to fly. That in-between time — often two to six weeks — is best spent somewhere calm, private and within easy reach of the hospital, in case a dressing needs changing or a scan needs repeating. A good recuperation base is not a holiday. It is part of the clinical journey.

rows.label: What to look for
rows.value: Proximity first: minutes from the treating hospital, not across a city. Then the practical things — step-free access, a lift, a room you can rest in during the day, gentle food, and staff who are unhurried and discreet. Serviced residences and apartment-hotels often suit longer stays better than a standard hotel: a small kitchen, space for a family member, and a sense of normal life while you heal.

rows.label: The options, broadly
rows.value: Three shapes tend to work. Hospital-affiliated guest accommodation or 'patient hotels', which sit closest to care and are used to medical routines. Serviced residences and apartment-hotels for two-week-plus stays with family. And, for those who want it, established recovery retreats that pair a nurse or physiotherapist with hotel-grade comfort. Each has a place; the right one depends on the procedure and how much support you'll want on hand.

rows.label: Bringing family
rows.value: Recovery is easier with the right person nearby. Plan a room or residence that comfortably holds a spouse or adult child, and think ahead about their needs too — a quiet place to work, meals, a way to get to and from the hospital. For longer stays, a two-bedroom serviced apartment is often calmer than two hotel rooms.

rows.label: How we arrange it
rows.value: We match the stay to the hospital and the procedure — location, access, food, length — and hold it alongside your treatment dates, so the move from ward to residence is seamless. Nursing or physiotherapy support at the residence can be arranged where clinically appropriate, coordinated with your treating team, never in place of them.

items: Evacuation moves you to proper care; repatriation brings you home — both are clinically decided.

rows.label: Two different things
rows.value: Medical evacuation moves a critically ill or injured person to the nearest facility that can properly treat them — sometimes across a city, sometimes across a border. Repatriation brings a stabilised patient home for continued care near family and their regular doctors. Both may use an air ambulance, a medically-equipped commercial flight, or ground transport, depending on the situation.

rows.label: Who decides, and how
rows.value: The decision is clinical, not logistical. The treating doctor on the ground and the assistance company's medical team decide together that transfer is medically necessary and safe, then arrange the appropriate transport with medical staff on board. With insurance or a membership, evacuation typically must be pre-authorised through the provider's assistance network — you generally cannot arrange your own air ambulance and claim it back. Notify the assistance line early; many policies expect contact within 24 to 48 hours.

rows.label: What it costs, and cover
rows.value: Air ambulance cost depends on distance and the medical equipment required, and international evacuations can be very expensive — commonly cited figures for cross-border cases run into six figures in US dollars. This is why dedicated membership programmes (such as Medjet or Global Rescue) and travel-insurance evacuation cover exist. Standard guidance suggests substantial evacuation cover for international travel; treat any figure as indicative and confirm your own policy limits and exclusions.

rows.label: Be ready before you need it
rows.value: Carry the assistance line's number and your policy or membership details where you can reach them instantly. Keep your key medical information and current medications to hand. Know the local emergency number at your destination. In a crisis, the first call is to local emergency services for immediate stabilisation; the assistance company is then looped in to coordinate transfer.

rows.label: How we help
rows.value: We help you put appropriate evacuation and repatriation cover in place before you travel, and we stay reachable if something happens — coordinating with your assistance provider, the hospital and your family, and lining up onward care in India. The clinical decisions rest with the doctors and the assistance medical team; we make the machinery around them move quickly.

items: Fertility law varies sharply by country and by your exact situation — take legal advice in both the destination and India.
Standard IVF is widely legal; donor rules (access, anonymity, age) differ by country.
India allows only altruistic surrogacy for eligible citizens, not for foreign intended parents.

This guide describes the landscape only; it is not legal, medical or ethical advice.

rows.label: Read this first
rows.value: Fertility law is complex, changes often, and turns on your exact circumstances — marital status, whether donor gametes or a surrogate are involved, and your own citizenship. This is a map, not advice. Before committing to any path or country, take qualified legal counsel in both the destination and India. What follows describes the landscape as reported; it does not recommend a route.

rows.label: IVF and donor conception
rows.value: Standard IVF is widely available and legal across most established destinations. Rules diverge on the details: who may access treatment, and how donors are handled. Spain, for example, permits assisted reproduction for single women and same-sex couples and operates anonymous egg donation under Law 14/2006, with large donor pools and short waits. The United Kingdom, by contrast, allows donor-conceived people to learn the donor's identity at 18. Age limits, donor anonymity and eligibility all vary — verify the current position of any clinic and country before you proceed.

rows.label: Surrogacy — the sharp differences
rows.value: This is where law diverges most, and where the risk of getting it wrong is highest. India permits only altruistic surrogacy, restricted to eligible Indian citizens, and does not offer it to foreign intended parents. Among destinations that allow surrogacy for non-residents, parts of the United States (California in particular) offer commercial gestational surrogacy with strong legal protection and clear parentage orders, while other jurisdictions such as Georgia permit it under narrower conditions. The global trend since 2020 has been toward restriction, not liberalisation, and there is no international legal standard. Parentage, citizenship and bringing a child home to India each require specialist legal advice.

rows.label: Bringing a child home
rows.value: A path that is lawful abroad still has to work under Indian law when you return — for the child's citizenship, parentage and travel documents. This is precisely where couples are caught out. Resolve it in advance with lawyers on both sides before any treatment begins, not after a child is born.

rows.label: How we help
rows.value: We help you reach reputable, verifiable clinics and experienced legal counsel in the relevant countries, and coordinate the practical journey — travel, stays, discretion. We describe the landscape; we do not give legal, medical or ethical advice, and every route should be confirmed with qualified professionals before you commit.

rows.value: For many patients, the answer is a commercial flight with a nurse or doctor accompanying you. It suits those who are stable but need monitoring, medication, or support in transit. rows.value: A dedicated air ambulance is for patients who cannot safely travel in a normal cabin, for example those needing a ventilator, IV drips, or cardiac monitoring. It carries a full medical team and equipment. It is the highest level of care in the air, and priced accordingly.

rows.label: Choosing the right level

rows.label: Pre-existing conditions are the crux
rows.value: A pre-existing condition is one you have consulted a doctor about or taken medication for before the policy starts. Insurers handle these in a few ways: they exclude the condition, apply a moratorium (a waiting period, often around 24 months, before it may be covered), or cover it at a higher premium. If the reason you are travelling is a known condition, read this section first.

rows.label: Declare everything, exactly
rows.value: Always declare your medical history accurately. Withholding information may feel tempting but tends to backfire at the moment of a claim. Continuous cover with no gaps also matters, as even a short lapse can reset waiting periods.

rows.label: What to confirm in writing
rows.value: Check the coverage limit, whether your specific treatment and hospital are in-network, and whether the insurer pays the hospital directly or reimburses you later. For Schengen and Germany, note that a category C visa needs travel health insurance of at least EUR 30,000 for the whole stay.

rows.label: The gaps to watch
rows.value: Look for limits on repatriation and air ambulance, on companion costs, and on complications of a planned procedure. Some 'stability' clauses require your condition to have been settled for 6 to 12 months. Ask for the exact wording, not a summary.

rows.label: Being understood
rows.value: Consent, symptoms, side-effects — these are not conversations to have through guesswork. Most top international hospitals provide professional medical interpreters, often at no cost to the patient, either in person for scheduled appointments or by video. Cleveland Clinic, for instance, provides interpreters at no cost and offers video remote interpreting across its hospitals. Ask for a Hindi or regional-language interpreter in advance so one is confirmed for your key consultations.

rows.label: Vegetarian and Jain food, on the ward
rows.value: Hospital food is part of recovery, and dietary needs are routine for good international-patient teams. Mount Elizabeth in Singapore, for example, tells patients not to worry about dietary or religious meals and to inform them of any special diet in advance. For strict vegetarian, Jain (no root vegetables), or satvik requirements, state the specifics clearly and early — 'vegetarian' can mean different things in different kitchens. Where the hospital cannot fully meet a strict requirement, meals can be arranged from a trusted outside source.

rows.label: The small comforts that matter
rows.value: A familiar routine helps. Prayer or meditation time, a quiet room, food that tastes of home, a family member allowed to stay longer — these are worth asking for, and most centres accommodate them. Bring what grounds you. Tell the international-patient office what matters to you; they arrange far more than most patients think to ask.

rows.value: Before you travel we confirm language support for your consultations and put your dietary requirements in writing to the hospital, with the specifics spelled out. items: Most destinations want doctors' letters (home and abroad), proof of funds, and intent to return.
The US uses the B-2 visa and can have very long interview waits from India, so start early.
The UK uses the Standard Visitor visa; Schengen needs EUR 30,000 travel health insurance.
Companion or attendant visas exist for most destinations, usually applied for alongside the patient.

rows.label: The common thread
rows.value: Nearly every destination wants the same core proof: a letter from a doctor at home, a letter or appointment confirmation from the treating hospital abroad, evidence you can fund the treatment, and an intention to return. A companion or attendant usually applies alongside you on a linked application. Rules change, so confirm current requirements before you apply.

rows.label: United States
rows.value: Travel for treatment is on the B-2 visitor visa. You will typically need a diagnosis from your Indian doctor, a letter from the US physician or hospital confirming treatment, and proof of funds to cover it. Interview appointment waits in India can be very long, so plan far ahead; an attendant applies separately as a B-2 visitor.

rows.label: United Kingdom
rows.value: There is no separate medical visa; you apply for the Standard Visitor visa for medical reasons. It is usually up to six months and can extend to eleven if a medical letter confirms longer treatment. Expect to show doctors' letters from home and the UK, that arrangements and funds are in place, and that you will leave when treatment ends.

rows.label: Schengen and Germany
rows.value: For short stays you apply for a Schengen (category C) visa for medical treatment. The German facility must confirm the treatment is medically necessary, and you need travel health insurance of at least EUR 30,000 for the stay. A visa can be issued for an accompanying person where a certificate confirms you must be accompanied; apply no later than 15 working days before travel.

rows.label: Singapore
rows.value: Indian passport holders need a visa in advance and cannot use visa-on-arrival. There is no separate medical category; you apply through VFS Global or the ICA e-Service with the usual documents plus your hospital's appointment confirmation. Processing is quick, but submit the SG Arrival Card before you land.

rows.label: Thailand
rows.value: Thailand offers a Medical Treatment visa. Many applicants can now apply through the official Thai e-Visa portal. You will need a letter from the Thai hospital detailing the treatment plan, proof of funds, and a passport valid at least six months. The stay can be extended at an immigration office with a letter from your treating physician.

rows.label: UAE (Dubai)
rows.value: A medical treatment entry permit is sponsored by the hospital, typically allowing entry within 60 days and a stay of up to 90 days, extendable once with a certified medical report. Companion permits are available, generally up to two per patient. Dubai has also announced a 'smart medical visa' linking approval to the hospital intake, launched in June 2026.

rows.value: For children, look for a dedicated children's hospital or a major centre with a strong paediatric department in the relevant specialty, and an international-patient team experienced with families. Ask about child-friendly wards, play and schooling support during long stays, and whether a parent can stay overnight on the ward. These are not extras for a child; they are part of the care.

rows.value: Children settle faster when things feel familiar. rows.label: Discretion is a discipline, not a favour
rows.value: Privacy holds when it is designed in from the first enquiry — not requested at the door. That means limiting who knows, controlling how records move, choosing where you stay and how you arrive, and keeping your name out of the chain. Done quietly. Done on purpose.

rows.label: Your data, and the law
rows.value: In India, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 makes consent the centre of how your health data may be collected and used — it must be free, specific, informed and unambiguous, and you may withdraw it. Hospitals abroad operate under their own regimes (such as HIPAA in the United States or GDPR in Europe). The practical point: know who holds your records, on what basis, and how to have them corrected or erased. We keep that chain tight and documented.

rows.label: Practical measures

All clinical decisions rest with accredited providers and your own physicians. Costs shown are indicative; a formal quote follows evaluation.

concierge.heading: Let us walk this path with you, step by step.
concierge.shareText: Share as little or as much as you wish. A single named person coordinates your flights, the stay near the clinic and your visa — start to safe return.
concierge.confidenceNote: Confidential. Discreet. Handled by a named human.

whereToBegin.lede: Transplant is among the most demanding journeys in medicine, bound tightly by clinical need, eligibility and law. This pathway helps you understand your options honestly and reach a leading transplant centre, with the realities set out plainly rather than smoothed over. Every clinical and eligibility decision rests with the transplant team.

steps.title: Share your records
steps.text: Your complete file is organised for review, as transplant centres assess candidacy carefully and thoroughly before anything else.

steps.title: Expert evaluation
steps.text: A transplant team reviews your case to advise on candidacy and the pathway open to you. We are candid about what is and is not possible, including donor and eligibility realities.

steps.title: Understand the rules
steps.text: Transplant is tightly regulated, and rules on donation and international patients differ by country. We help you understand the legal and ethical framework of each option clearly, and only pursue routes that are proper and above board.

steps.title: Choose the centre
steps.text: Where a route is open, you weigh leading transplant centres across the US, Germany, Singapore and India against the clinical and practical realities.

steps.title: Travel, treatment & extended stay
steps.text: Transplant asks for a longer, carefully supported stay for you and your family, which we arrange end to end — the visa, the flights and the accommodation. Interpreters and diet are set with the hospital.

steps.title: Continuity back home
steps.text: Long-term follow-up is essential after transplant, and we help hand the immunosuppression and monitoring plan cleanly to your physicians in India.

whereToBegin.note: Indicative only and firmly on evaluation. Transplant costs are substantial, highly case-specific and inseparable from eligibility, so we never quote in the abstract. We share figures only once a centre has evaluated candidacy and set out the full pathway.
